usageNote: A relaxed, everyday greeting used between friends and age-mates, similar in tone to "what's up?" in English.
The standard reply to a greeting. Polite in nearly every setting, from family to strangers.
Used when meeting someone for the first time; a natural follow-up after the initial greeting.
A humble way to explain you're still picking up the language when someone speaks quickly.
Called out to invite family or guests to the table; refusing a meal invitation is considered impolite.
A direct, practical request. Useful phrase for a guest to know in any household.
Literally references the sun's position; a reminder that time was traditionally tracked by daylight.
Common after farm work or a long walk; often followed by an offer to rest or sit.
Reflects daily life near the Kavango River, where fetching water is still a shared household task.
Elders are addressed with warmth and respect; family terms are used often even for close non-relatives.
Also used respectfully toward older men in the community, not only a biological father.
A single term covers brothers and sisters; context or a name usually clarifies which.
Used to speak respectfully about parents, grandparents, or community elders collectively.
The base counting word; Rukwangali numbers beyond ten often borrow structure from Bantu number systems.
Used both for counting objects and people.
Follows the same counting pattern as "vali"; useful when bargaining at a local market.

rukwangali: Kambungu kamwe hamu kanyata mema gendji
english: One small basket does not hold much water
usageNote: A saying about limits and preparation — used to caution against under-preparing for a task.

rukwangali: Mbudi zongwa kapi zi hepa mbili
english: Good news does not need to be repeated twice
usageNote: Suggests that truth and good conduct speak for themselves without needing to be forced.
